/-!
# Magic Squares

*References:*

* [Magic Square of Squares - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_square_of_squares)
* [multimagie.com](http://www.multimagie.com/English/SquaresOfSquaresSearch.htm)
* [Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
* [Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
-/

namespace MagicSquares

/--
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ matrix such that every entry is a distinct square,
and all rows, columns, and diagonals add up to the same value?

0 is excluded, as a Magic Square of Squares with 0 and 8 distinct squares is know is knownn.
See [Magic Square of Squares](https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem exists_magic_square_squares :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ m : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ, ∃ t : ℕ,
       m.Injective2 ∧
       (∀ i j, 0 < (m i j) ∧ IsSquare (m i j)) ∧
       (∀ i, ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧
       (∀ j, ∑ i, m i j = t) ∧
       m 0 0 + m 1 1 + m 2 2 = t ∧
       m 0 2 + m 1 1 + m 2 0 = t := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist a $3 \times 3$ semi-magic square whose entries are all distinct positive
integer cubes? A square is semi-magic if all rows and columns sum to the same total.

More precisely, we seek a $3 \times 3$ matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that each
$a_{ij} = n_{ij}^3$ for some positive integer $n_{ij}$, all nine cubes are distinct,
and all row sums and column sums are equal.

*Reference:*
[Semi-Magic Square of Cubes](https://unsolvedproblems.org/index_files/SquareofCubes.htm)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem exists_semi_magic_square_cubes :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ m : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ, ∃ t : ℕ,
       m.Injective2 ∧
       (∀ i j, ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ m i j = n ^ 3) ∧
       (∀ i, ∑ j, m i j = t) ∧
       (∀ j, ∑ i, m i j = t) := by
  sorry

end MagicSquares

findings.description: The docstring's assertion that a magic square of squares containing zero and eight distinct squares is known repeats an error in Gardner's original article. The known examples are only semi-magic, not magic with both diagonals as required here. In fact, a full 3×3 magic square of distinct integer squares cannot contain zero. The Lean statement itself is faithful: its positivity requirement is redundant, not an exclusion needed to avoid a known solution.
findings.source_evidence: Gardner, “The magic of 3×3,” Quantum 6(3), p. 25 (https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N3.pdf), originally says: “Such squares exist with eight distinct squares plus a zero.” He explicitly corrects this in “The latest magic,” Quantum 6(4), p. 60 (https://static.nsta.org/pdfs/QuantumV6N4.pdf): “In my article I said that order-3 squares made of squares are possible with zero in one cell. I should have added that squares of this type are magic only in rows and columns.”
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the erroneous sentence with an explanation that allowing zero gives an equivalent problem because a full 3×3 magic square of distinct squares cannot contain zero. If retaining the historical discussion, distinguish semi-magic examples and cite Gardner's correction. No change to the Lean theorem is necessary.

reformulations.difference: Lean explicitly requires every square entry to be positive, whereas the source's formulation using nine distinct integer squares does not separately exclude zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write the center as c². The eight magic-line equations imply t = 3c² and that every pair of opposite entries sums to 2c². A zero entry therefore forces another square d² = 2c², which is possible over the integers only when c = d = 0. Then t = 0, so all nonnegative entries vanish, contradicting distinctness. Thus every admissible square already has positive entries. Conversely, a positive-entry solution is immediately a nonnegative-entry solution. The exact equivalence between the natural-number predicates with and without positivity was proved as ReviewZero.allowing_zero_iff_positive in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
